title: Ron And Jammy

jokes.text: I just farted.
jokes.setup: Leslie greets Jamm with 'Knopey, my girl, wuddup?' — a casual, friendly opener suggesting a normal reunion
jokes.punchline: Jamm's first words are a completely flat, matter-of-fact declaration that he just farted
jokes.explanation: The joke lands because of pure economy and character — Jamm's complete lack of self-awareness is perfectly encapsulated in three words. It's a great cold-open beat that immediately re-establishes the character. Not exceptional writing but well-executed deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: Hey Leslie!

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: I just farted.

jokes.text: human equivalent of gas station sushi, Jeremy Jamm
jokes.setup: Leslie is in a talking-head confessional describing the deciding vote on the city council
jokes.punchline: She describes Jamm as 'the human equivalent of gas station sushi'
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional insult comedy. 'Gas station sushi' is a perfectly specific, disgusting image — it captures someone who is technically available, untrustworthy in quality, and makes you feel vaguely ill. It's vivid, economical, and completely in Leslie's voice. It approaches the 8.0 anchor standard: highly quotable, character-specific, original construction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jeremy Jamm is like if a mayonnaise jar came to life and decided to ruin everything good about government.

jokes.text: Before we go any further, I need to ask my girlfriend how she wants me to vote.
jokes.setup: Leslie has come to lobby Jamm for his vote on a zoning issue — a straightforward political ask
jokes.punchline: Jamm says he needs to check with his girlfriend first, immediately undermining any authority he might have
jokes.explanation: Solid setup for the Tammy reveal. The joke itself is functional — we're curious who the girlfriend is, and the beat where he asks is amusing — but it's really just a delivery mechanism for the bigger punchline coming.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jeremy and Tammy are dating? Their combined name sounds like a food product. Jemmy. It's a breakfast spread.

jokes.text: Hello, Leslie. / Tammy. [long pause / reaction beat] Wow. Jamm and Tammy! 'Jammy.'
jokes.setup: Jamm says he needs to consult his girlfriend; Leslie asks who it is
jokes.punchline: Tammy Two (Ron's terrifying ex-wife) steps out, and Leslie's stunned silence gives way to her processing it with the involuntary nickname 'Jammy'
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Tammy Two is with Jamm is a genuine shock moment with enormous comedic payoff. The roughly 30-second gap in dialogue (the [01:09] timestamp beat) represents Leslie's silent processing, which IS the joke. Then 'Jammy' — Leslie's brain immediately workshopping the couple name despite her horror — is perfectly in character. This earns high scores because the structure is immaculate and it sets up the entire episode's conflict.

jokes.text: Wow. Jamm and Tammy! 'Jammy.' Jammy.
jokes.setup: The shocking reveal that Jamm is dating Tammy
jokes.punchline: Leslie's brain immediately latches onto the portmanteau — 'Jammy' — and she says it with delight, momentarily forgetting to be horrified
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie character comedy — she can't help but find the couple name adorable even when the situation is horrifying. The repetition of 'Jammy' as it sinks in is perfectly timed. High character integration because only Leslie would geek out on the wordplay in this moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, when did we start dating?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, no. No no no no no. That's not... we're not... I mean, I love you, but not like that. You're like a brother to me. A really annoying brother who I'm forced to work with and who keeps making terrible decisions.

jokes.text: You guys are so cute. When did you... Why would either one of you, you know... Why? Dear God, why?
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been confronted with the reality of the Jamm/Tammy relationship
jokes.punchline: Her attempt to be polite immediately collapses into existential horror as she cannot complete a coherent sentence
jokes.explanation: The escalating fragmentation of Leslie's speech — from polite inquiry to unfinished thoughts to pure theological pleading — is a great character moment. The rhythm of the deterioration is well-written. Leslie's simultaneous politeness reflex and genuine horror are perfectly captured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, Joan, Chateau Marmont is a hotel in Los Angeles. You can't drink a hotel.

jokes.text: Hit it off at karaoke. She saw me nail Gangsta's Paradise, I saw her bite the door guy. She then let me buy her a bunch of purses. And the rest is history. A bunch.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks how Jamm and Tammy got together
jokes.punchline: The story escalates from normal karaoke flirting to Tammy biting a man, to 'a bunch' of purses repeated for emphasis
jokes.explanation: This is great economy comedy. 'I saw her bite the door guy' is a perfectly absurd detail delivered flatly as if it's charming courtship behavior. The callback to 'a bunch' at the end (Jamm re-emphasizing the purse cost) shows Jamm's shallow character. Each sentence escalates the chaos while remaining perfectly in both characters' voices.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Did you get Buddy Holly to sing?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, he died in a plane crash in 1959.

jokes.text: Maybe you're not a blonde bimbo after all. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Leslie makes a political argument for why Tammy should vote for her (to hurt Ron)
jokes.punchline: Jamm calls her a blonde bimbo as backhanded acknowledgment, and Leslie genuinely thanks him
jokes.explanation: The double beat works well: Jamm's insult is both condescending and oddly sincere as his highest compliment, and Leslie accepting it as genuine praise reveals her tunnel vision on her goals. Two character truths land simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm April.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Nice to meet you, Erin.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's April.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Yes, dear, April. That's what I said.

jokes.text: Sure, I'm aligning myself with terrible people, but think of all the wonderful people who will benefit from a national park. It's worth it. And you can trust my opinion because I have a lot to gain by being right, and I have severe tunnel vision about achieving my goals.
jokes.setup: Leslie is doing a talking-head confessional justifying her alliance with Jamm and Tammy
jokes.punchline: She acknowledges her terrible judgment with complete self-awareness, then immediately undermines the self-awareness by citing her bias as a reason to trust her
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining logic ('trust my opinion because I'm biased') is classic Leslie — she has enough self-awareness to see her flaws but not enough to apply the lesson. It's a compact encapsulation of her character and the show's affectionate critique of her obsessive drive.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: The dark twist that it was just one car they had to fight over.

jokes.text: We couldn't get a bottle of Chateau Marmont because it's a hotel in Los Angeles, not a wine.
jokes.setup: Ben is apologizing to Joan Calamezzo for not being able to accommodate all her requests
jokes.punchline: One of her requests was a bottle of 'Chateau Marmont' — a famous hotel she apparently confused with a wine
jokes.explanation: Efficiently establishes Joan's oblivious celebrity diva character. The specificity of 'Chateau Marmont' (it sounds plausibly like a wine) makes the confusion believable while still being absurd. Ben's deadpan explanation is note-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What does culinary mean?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It means you're really good at lying about how much the meal costs.

jokes.text: Well, did you at least get Buddy Holly to sing? / No, because he's been famously dead for 60 years.
jokes.setup: Following the Chateau Marmont confusion, Joan asks another impossible request
jokes.punchline: She wants Buddy Holly to perform; Ben's response 'he's been famously dead for 60 years' emphasizes the absurdity with the word 'famously'
jokes.explanation: The word 'famously' is doing enormous work here — it's Ben's polite way of saying 'how do you not know this?' while remaining professional. The escalation from confusing a hotel for wine to not knowing Buddy Holly is dead perfectly builds Joan's character. A tight, well-constructed joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, Ron, that's a very sophisticated economic argument, but you know what? Your face is a sophisticated economic argument.

jokes.text: What? [Joan genuinely shocked that Buddy Holly is dead]
jokes.setup: Ben has just informed Joan that Buddy Holly has been dead for 60 years
jokes.punchline: Joan's single 'What?' implies she genuinely did not know this — her shock is played completely straight
jokes.explanation: A single word carrying maximum comedic payload. The reaction works because Joan's entire character — the delusional celebrity who exists in her own reality — is crystallized in one confused syllable.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Commissioner Gordon, people of Gotham.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Joan, this is Pawnee. You're the Parks Department secretary. You're having a psychotic break.

jokes.text: Hi, my name is April. And I'm your biggest fan and I pretty much hate everyone.
jokes.setup: April is introducing herself to Joan Calamezzo, a celebrity she admires
jokes.punchline: The standard fan declaration is immediately undercut by April's trademark misanthropic qualifier
jokes.explanation: Perfect April line — the juxtaposition of sincere fandom with reflexive misanthropy is quintessential character comedy. It's economical and couldn't be said by anyone else on the show.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jeremy, please don't mention Hitler.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: You know who I think is underrated? Hitler.

jokes.text: You said your name was Glenn? / Yes, I did.
jokes.setup: April just introduced herself as April to Joan
jokes.punchline: Joan calls her Glenn; April confirms this without hesitation
jokes.explanation: Both characters' voices converge perfectly: Joan is oblivious and self-centered, April is deadpan and contrarian. April immediately adopting the wrong name without missing a beat is both character-revealing and genuinely funny. 'Yes, I did' is the ideal three-word response. Strong 8 territory.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: His reasoning is pure mustache solidarity

jokes.text: She did a string of shows from rehab. Victoria Herzog, you were a successful attorney from Wilmington, Delaware. Then you hit rock bottom. / This is supposed to be anonymous.
jokes.setup: Ben describes Joan's erratic recent behavior — 'she's gone off the deep end'
jokes.punchline: Joan did shows FROM rehab, complete with ambushing patients about their rock bottoms while they expected anonymity
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the rehab patient from Wilmington, Delaware is a nice touch — it grounds an absurd scenario in mundane detail. The 'This is supposed to be anonymous' payoff is well-earned. Dark but not mean-spirited.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Follow your passion, do what makes you happy, pursue your dreams with everything you've got.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Now, let's talk about legalizing murder.

jokes.text: She once gave every member in her audience a car. One car, that they all had to fight for.
jokes.setup: Ben continues cataloguing Joan's increasingly unhinged show moments
jokes.punchline: The Oprah car giveaway parody is twisted — she gave ONE car for the whole audience to fight over
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the Joan sequence. The setup references the famous Oprah car giveaway (a deeply embedded cultural moment), then subverts it with the darkest possible twist — one car, whole audience, fight for it. The economy is perfect: the first sentence creates the reference, the second destroys it. Highly quotable, original, and the reversal is genuinely sharp. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dude, I've been looking through your Instagram followers. I found two really cute girls you should ask out.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Who?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Your cousin Madison and your aunt Jennifer.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Andy, those are my family members.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, but they're really hot.

jokes.text: She did a show where she called all of her ex-boyfriends while sitting on a washing machine.
jokes.setup: Ben continues the list of Joan's erratic show ideas
jokes.punchline: The 'sitting on a washing machine' detail implies vibration for... reasons, while the ex-boyfriend calls frame it as emotional chaos
jokes.explanation: A perfectly suggestive detail that works on two levels — the emotional messiness of drunk-dialing exes combined with the physical implication of the washing machine. The writers trust the audience to make the connection without spelling it out.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So Tom, I was looking at your Instagram and I noticed it's just pictures of your family. Don't you have any friends?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have friends.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: On Instagram?

jokes.text: I love her so much. I hope she's my real mom.
jokes.setup: April and Ben have been watching clips of Joan's increasingly unhinged behavior
jokes.punchline: April's response is sincere admiration, topped by hoping Joan is her real mother — implying this chaos is her ideal parental figure
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character economy. The two-sentence beat tells us everything about April: she is drawn to chaos and dysfunction, views normalcy with contempt, and her sincerity in this moment is both funny and character-revealing. 'I hope she's my real mom' is a genuine laugh-out-loud line that is completely, uniquely April.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you absolute snook! You snookered us out of that vote!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're a snook-faced snook with snookish intentions!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is the snookiest snookery I've ever seen from a snook!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Knope, 'snook' isn't even a word.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well it is NOW, Ron. You snook that word into existence!

jokes.text: Tom. What does culinary mean? / It means it's a cause for celebration. Round of drinks for everyone, on the house!
jokes.setup: Tom is reading a magazine article that calls him an 'entrepreneur bachelor' in the culinary world
jokes.punchline: Tom has no idea what 'culinary' means and interprets it as generically positive, declaring a party
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Tom's grandiosity and intellectual shallowness are well-integrated. The 'Round of drinks for everyone, on the house!' as a non-sequitur response to not understanding a word is a fun beat. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, what about a snook where you do it, but backwards? So it's a koons.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Or a snook where you're underwater. That's a snorkel.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A snook in space would be a... sn-ooooook.

jokes.text: Let me also get a chicken parm and a lasagna on the side. And a spaghetti to go. On the house!
jokes.setup: Tom has just declared a round of free drinks for everyone at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to ordering a large personal meal and declaring that free too
jokes.explanation: The escalation from generous gesture to personal gluttony works because it reveals Tom's self-centeredness under the performative generosity. The specific Italian food order adds some flavor. Competent but not special.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: Did it work? Did you vote for me?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: I knew my vagina could get you to do anything.

jokes.text: Are you bummed, Tom? / Hey, I got a quick fix for that. Let's get hammered. Everything here is free.
jokes.setup: Tom has just admitted to feeling lonely after seeing the 'bachelor' label in print
jokes.punchline: His solution to emotional emptiness is immediately 'let's get hammered' — and he frames 'everything is free' as the kicker reason
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat. Tom's emotional avoidance through hedonism is on-brand but the joke itself isn't particularly crafted — it's a well-worn 'drink to forget' premise. The 'everything is free' addendum is the only fresh element.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: Did my seduction work? Did I seduce you back into my uterus?

jokes.text: How's that zero-dollar bid coming along? / You know, in my experience with capitalism, people would normally expect money in exchange for their goods and land. / In my experience with butt faces, you are one.
jokes.setup: Leslie confronts Ron about his Gryzzl bid for the Newport land
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers a mock-serious economic argument; Leslie responds with a kindergarten-level insult delivered with complete commitment
jokes.explanation: The structure is near-perfect: Ron's response is a lofty, measured observation phrased like a business school maxim, and Leslie's comeback matches the cadence exactly ('In my experience with butt faces...') but with a child's insult. The parallel construction elevates what would be a simple joke into something formally clever. 'You are one' as the flat landing is ideal. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Trying to separate Jamm from Tammy is like trying to separate a remora fish from a shark. Except the shark is also named Tammy and she's already eaten your car and your house and your will to live.

jokes.text: Well, I'm convinced. Tomorrow I'm voting for Gryzzl.
jokes.setup: Ron has just begun his presentation for the Newport property rezoning — he's barely said anything
jokes.punchline: A councilman immediately declares himself convinced after Ron's first, incomplete sentence
jokes.explanation: A solid subversion of the expected hearing format — Ron's reputation or delivery is apparently so compelling that deliberation is unnecessary. Works as a quick beat but the joke is over quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wow, Chicago! The Big Apple!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's New York.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: You know who else had a plan? / Please don't say Hitler. / Adolf Hitler!
jokes.setup: Leslie protests that she hasn't gotten a chance to present her plan; the councilman asks rhetorically 'you know who else had a plan?'
jokes.punchline: Leslie preemptively asks him not to say Hitler; he says Hitler anyway
jokes.explanation: The joke is elevated by Leslie's preemptive 'Please don't say Hitler' — she KNOWS where this is going and it still happens. The inevitability is part of the comedy. The councilman following with 'Adolf Hitler!' (using the full name, solemnly) adds an extra beat of absurdity. Well-structured Godwin's Law joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. You can't just show up at her workplace unannounced. That's crazy. You need a strategic plan. First, you case the joint. Find out her schedule, her routine, which exits she uses. Then you wait in the bushes outside her office building until she arrives.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Tom, that's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then when she least expects it, you jump out and surprise her. She'll love it. Trust me.

jokes.text: I'm with Swanson. It's a stache thing. Stache bros. You wouldn't understand.
jokes.setup: Following the Hitler comparison, another councilman announces his vote for Ron
jokes.punchline: His reasoning is purely mustache solidarity — 'stache bros'
jokes.explanation: The absurdist logic of mustache-based political solidarity is delightfully specific. 'You wouldn't understand' adds the mock-exclusivity of a secret brotherhood. Quick and punchy.

jokes.text: Thank you, Commissioner Gordon, people of Gotham. / Okay. She thinks she's in Batman.
jokes.setup: Joan is attending the hearing and appears to be fully confused about what is happening around her
jokes.punchline: She addresses the room as if they are characters from Batman; Ben's deadpan explanation to the camera confirms the absurdity
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Commissioner Gordon' rather than generic Batman reference is perfect. Ben's talking-head 'she thinks she's in Batman' delivers the premise with maximum efficiency. A strong absurdist Joan moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be a professional kazoo player.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Andy, that's not a real job.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What do you mean? People play kazoos all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, at like, children's birthday parties. Not as a career.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, where do you think kazoos come from? There's gotta be someone playing them professionally somewhere.

jokes.text: On a separate note, I think that America should have a purge night. Let me explain why.
jokes.setup: Joan has just delivered an apparently inspiring speech about loving what you do and passion
jokes.punchline: She pivots without transition to advocating for a national purge — the tonal whiplash is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'On a separate note' is doing incredible work — the transition phrase that pretends this is a normal pivot. The Purge reference is culturally specific and dark, and the 'Let me explain why' suggesting there IS a coherent argument is the capper. Well-constructed tonal whiplash comedy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If the whole government thing doesn't work out, I'm going to become a professional chess player who specializes in underwater basket weaving strategies.

jokes.text: I must be the first person ever to have money, power, and notoriety, but still feel empty.
jokes.setup: Tom is having a talking-head about feeling lonely despite his success
jokes.punchline: He presents this as a unique, unprecedented insight — completely unaware that this is one of humanity's oldest feelings
jokes.explanation: Tom's complete lack of self-awareness that he's experiencing the world's most clichéd rich-person problem is well-captured. 'I must be the first person ever' is the key phrase — his narcissism prevents him from recognizing this is a universal condition.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have to quit my job.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm going to become a professional dead body for medical students to practice on. It's the only job where my natural coldness is actually an asset.

jokes.text: What about her? / She's cute. Date her. / That's my cousin. / How about her? / That's my dad! / What's wrong with you? / I'm drunk, okay?
jokes.setup: Andy is drunkenly helping Tom browse Gryzzl (social media) to find a potential partner
jokes.punchline: Andy's suggestions are Tom's cousin and then his father; when confronted, Andy's defense is 'I'm drunk, okay?'
jokes.explanation: The escalation from cousin to father (getting worse) with Andy's non-apology 'I'm drunk, okay?' is well-paced. The 'Why are you only friends with your family?' follow-up adds a nice beat. Andy's oblivious enthusiasm is well-deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Do you remember what Joan said?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, she said 'I'm just a girl standing in front of a boy asking him to love her.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not what she said.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, that's what I'm going with.

jokes.text: Was she in Destiny's Child?
jokes.setup: Tom mentions he used to date Lucy and was really into her; Andy is trying to place why she looks familiar
jokes.punchline: Andy's best theory for why a woman looks familiar is that she might have been in Destiny's Child
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Destiny's Child' as Andy's mental shorthand for 'attractive woman I might know' is perfect Andy comedy. It reveals his cultural reference points while being completely unhelpful. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.line: Classic funeral home pun

jokes.text: Do you realize what's happening? We've been sitting here searching for your soul mate this whole time and then Lucy just Gryzzl-texts you out of nowhere? It's a sign! And we have to catch it.
jokes.setup: Lucy has messaged Tom on Gryzzl out of nowhere
jokes.punchline: Andy's breathless, movie-logic interpretation of this coincidence, complete with 'we have to catch it' (signs apparently being catchable objects)
jokes.explanation: 'We have to catch it' as a modification of the 'it's a sign' cliché — treating the sign as a physical object requiring pursuit — is the freshest element here. Andy's romantic-comedy logic is charming but the joke is moderately crafted.

jokes.text: No, you got all sneaky and snuck around and snooked that vote away from me. And I know this because earlier I sneaked and snooked around... The snooker has become the snorked!
jokes.setup: Leslie accuses Ron of undermining her by getting to Jamm first
jokes.punchline: In her anger, Leslie invents increasingly nonsensical past-tenses and transforms 'snooker' into 'snorked' as the triumphant revelation
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The escalating verbal deterioration — snuck, snooked, snorked — mirrors Leslie's escalating emotional state. 'The snooker has become the snorked' is delivered with total confidence as if it's a real idiom. The joke is fully earned through character (Leslie's tendency to commit fully to whatever she's saying, even nonsense) and formally clever as wordplay. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: She controls what I eat. She has a list of approved foods taped to the inside of the refrigerator. If I try to eat anything that's not on the list, she physically stops me.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: Last week I tried to have a yogurt that wasn't on the list. She chased me around the kitchen with a spatula.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: She actually follows me to restaurants and checks the ingredients of everything I order with the manager.

jokes.text: She's near. [Ron senses Tammy's presence]
jokes.setup: Ron, Leslie, and Jamm are in mid-conversation
jokes.punchline: Ron suddenly stops, alert like an animal, and simply says 'She's near' — as if Tammy Two is a supernatural predator
jokes.explanation: Two words carrying enormous comedic weight. The joke requires total knowledge of Ron and Tammy's mythology — Ron, the most stoic man alive, reduced to a prey animal by his ex. The implication that he has developed a Tammy-sense like a trauma response is both funny and deeply character-consistent. Economy score of 9.5 for two words doing the work of a paragraph.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The existence of such a ridiculous status symbol

jokes.text: You've always been against me and Ron. You're a big part of the reason that he and I aren't together, and I had to settle for this placeholder. / I love you so much.
jokes.setup: Tammy is defending her decision to vote for Ron to Leslie
jokes.punchline: She calls Jamm her 'placeholder' for Ron — and Jamm's response is immediate, unconditional 'I love you so much'
jokes.explanation: The cruelty of 'placeholder' lands hard, and Jamm's immediate love declaration in response demonstrates exactly how broken he already is. The joke works on cringe and dark levels simultaneously — it's genuinely awful and perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: She makes me miserable. She belittles me constantly. She won't let me have any friends. She controls my money. She hates everything I love. She's mean to my family. She makes me sleep in the garage.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: And yet... this feels right.

jokes.text: Did it work, baby? Are you horny with gratitude?
jokes.setup: Leslie has deduced that Tammy voted for Ron hoping to win him back
jokes.punchline: Tammy asks Ron if her gambit has made him 'horny with gratitude' — a phrase that is both perfectly Tammy and completely unhinged
jokes.explanation: 'Horny with gratitude' is a genuinely great construction — no one else in television has said this phrase, and no character other than Tammy Two could deliver it. It's specific, unsettling, and hilarious. The combination of sexuality and transactional manipulation in four words is a perfect Tammy encapsulation. High quotability and character integration score.

dialogue.line: Physical manifestation of his stress getting worse

jokes.text: It's like rescuing a bunny from a lion. But that lion is a demonic sociopath with really nice cleavage.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in a talking-head describing the challenge of breaking Jamm free from Tammy
jokes.punchline: The bunny/lion metaphor is extended with the specific qualifier 'demonic sociopath with really nice cleavage' — acknowledging Tammy's physical appeal as a tactical weapon
jokes.explanation: The extension of the metaphor to include 'really nice cleavage' is the key move — Leslie acknowledging Tammy's physical power as a legitimate threat, delivered in her earnest briefing style. The cleavage detail coming from Leslie specifically (not a male character) is character-intelligent writing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you haven't seen Monsters, Inc.? How is that even possible? It's a Pixar masterpiece! Mike Wazowski? Boo? The door factory? These are cultural touchstones! You can't just live in a cabin and ignore the entire canon of modern animation. What else haven't you seen? Have you seen Toy Story? Finding Nemo? Do you even know who Elmo is? Because I'm starting to think you've been living under a rock, and not even a cool, artisanal rock that you sourced yourself. This is a problem, Ron. A real problem.

jokes.text: That'll be $830. / Oh, no! This is so dumb! / Oh, awesome. Turn the car around. We're going back home. / No way. Pay me. And get the hell outta my cab.
jokes.setup: Andy announced they were going to Chicago; they apparently got in a cab
jokes.punchline: The cab fare is $830 — they drove to Chicago in a cab from Indiana
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Andy's 'we're going to Chicago' impulse decision — they actually took a cab, which is both entirely believable for these characters and appropriately insane. The $830 number is specific enough to feel real. Tom's immediate reversal ('turn the car around') is a good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I have a gold bar.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Wait, why is it shaped like a bar?

jokes.text: Chicago! The big apple.
jokes.setup: Andy and Tom have arrived in Chicago after the cab ride
jokes.punchline: Andy celebrates their arrival by giving Chicago New York City's nickname
jokes.explanation: A classic Andy malapropsim — he enthusiastically uses the wrong city's nickname. Simple and quick, but character-perfect. Andy's geographic/cultural confusion is a well-established trait.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy is not a woman you can treat like a normal person. She's a war criminal. She should be tried at The Hague.

jokes.text: You can't not talk to someone for five years and then show up unannounced where they work in a different city. That's what murderers do before they murder someone.
jokes.setup: Andy suggests they should say hi to Lucy since they're already in Chicago
jokes.punchline: Tom argues against it by characterizing unannounced visits as pre-murder behavior
jokes.explanation: 'That's what murderers do before they murder someone' has a tautological quality that makes it funnier — the added 'before they murder someone' is technically redundant but rhythmically perfect. The escalation from social faux pas to murder is classically absurdist while feeling true to Tom's anxiety.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Jeremy, I don't want to hear about your sex life.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Ron, you're just jealous because Tammy and I have a very active sex life.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Active? Jeremy, I've seen more action at a DMV on a Sunday.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: That's not true! Tammy says I'm very...

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Tammy says a lot of things. None of them are about you.

jokes.text: You're not gonna murder me, are you?
jokes.setup: Lucy appears and Tom is stunned; she asks what he's doing there
jokes.punchline: Tom's first response to seeing Lucy is to ask if she's going to murder him — his own paranoid framing echoed back
jokes.explanation: The callback lands perfectly — Tom has immediately applied his own paranoid logic to the situation he's now in. The fact that he asks HER this (rather than defending himself) inverts the paranoia delightfully. Well-structured callback with excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You know what? Every job is just a way to avoid dealing with your actual problems. Mortician, astronaut, professional cuddler—doesn't matter. We're all just running from something.

jokes.text: He's here helping me find a place to live. I just got a job here. And then when you hit him up on Gryzzl, he was like, 'Let's go say hi to Lucy since we're already here in Chicago.' Yeah. That's the deal.
jokes.setup: Lucy asks what they're doing in Chicago; Andy improvises a cover story
jokes.punchline: Andy's lie is transparently false (Tom is not moving to Chicago) and Tom's flat 'Yeah, that's the deal' confirms the obvious lie
jokes.explanation: The complicity of Tom going along with the terrible lie is sweet and character-consistent. The lie is obviously thin, which is part of the comedy. Functional cringe-comedy setup for the scene but not exceptionally crafted.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You know what? Every job is just paperwork. Even being a mortician is just paperwork. You're literally just filing dead people.

jokes.text: Head coach of the Chicago Bulls. / No, he's working at a non-profit. / No. What? Am I? / Oh, that sucks.
jokes.setup: Lucy asks what Tom's new job in Chicago is (continuing the cover lie)
jokes.punchline: Andy says 'Head coach of the Chicago Bulls'; Tom corrects to 'non-profit'; Andy seems genuinely surprised he has a non-profit job; Lucy commiserates
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed four-beat joke. Andy's lie escalates from 'moving here' to 'head coach of the Bulls' — a wild overshoot. Tom's correction punctures it. Andy's 'No. What? Am I?' implies he may have forgotten/not known about his own situation. And Lucy's sincere 'Oh, that sucks' about non-profits is the perfect button. Four characters, four beats, excellent rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Tammy. I hate everything about you. Your face makes me want to commit a crime. Also, I'm going to steal your lunch and your dignity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: That's... that's not helping.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, you think this is bad? Wait until she makes you sit in silence while she eats an entire rotisserie chicken and stares at you with dead eyes.

jokes.text: Except hearing Joan talk about her passion and doing what you really love totally freaked me out. Eight years ago, I accepted a random internship at the parks department, and then Leslie told me to do a bunch of stuff, and now I'm executive director of regional whatever, and I don't even know what it means.
jokes.setup: Ben checks in on how April is doing
jokes.punchline: April describes her entire career arc as passively following Leslie's instructions to arrive at a title she doesn't understand
jokes.explanation: 'Leslie told me to do a bunch of stuff' as a career summary is perfectly April — she removes all agency from her own arc while simultaneously being accurate about how the character developed. 'Executive director of regional whatever' is a lovely self-deprecating title mangling.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She's been living in my attic for three weeks. She eats the insects that accumulate near the light fixture. She's made a nest out of my old tax documents and she only comes down at night to sharpen her nails on the wooden banister.

jokes.text: I have to quit. To do what? I'm just gonna go live under a bridge and ask people riddles before they cross.
jokes.setup: April says she has no idea what her purpose is and needs to make a change
jokes.punchline: Her alternative career plan is to become a bridge troll asking riddles
jokes.explanation: The bridge troll plan is delivered with total sincerity as April's genuine alternative career — it's specific enough (riddles, crossing) to feel like she's actually thought this through, which is the joke. No one else on the show could say this line. High economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to Boston. That's right, I'm going to Boston. Because that's what Chicago is — it's just Boston with worse accent and better food.

jokes.text: Do you remember what Joan said at the ceremony? That it doesn't count as stripping if no one pays you? / Yes, she did say that. But no.
jokes.setup: Ben tries to refocus April on the positive thing Joan said about passion
jokes.punchline: April correctly identifies a different (absurd) Joan quote; Ben has to validate it was real before redirecting
jokes.explanation: The callback structure here is exceptional. Joan apparently also said 'it doesn't count as stripping if no one pays you' at the ceremony — we never heard it, which makes it funnier (the writers trust us to accept it happened). Ben's 'Yes, she did say that. But no.' is perfectly structured: validating the absurd before redirecting. The pause implied by 'But no' is everything.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Lucy, I've been wanting to talk to you about something... something special.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: How would you like to come work for me at Entertainment 720?

jokes.text: Hi. I'm Ben, this is April. And I'm scared of death.
jokes.setup: Ben and April arrive at a mortuary and are greeted by the mortician Dan
jokes.punchline: Ben introduces himself and April, then adds an unsolicited personal disclosure about his fear of death
jokes.explanation: The overshare is perfectly timed — normal professional greeting suddenly derailed by personal anxiety. 'And I'm scared of death' as a third introduction item is excellent economy. Ben's neurosis is well-deployed.

jokes.text: You're gonna love it here. People are dying to get in.
jokes.setup: The mortician welcomes Ben and April to the mortuary
jokes.punchline: He delivers the world's most obvious mortuary pun with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: This is a deliberately hacky pun — the joke is partly that Dan uses the most tired mortuary pun imaginable. The deadpan delivery saves it slightly, but 'people are dying to get in' is the definition of a low-craft pun. It works in context as character establishment for Dan, but it's objectively weak writing being used intentionally.

jokes.text: Come on, come on. We'll start down at the cadaver chute!
jokes.setup: Dan is enthusiastically showing them around the mortuary
jokes.punchline: 'The cadaver chute' — delivered with the same enthusiasm as 'the snack bar' — is an absurdly mundane name for a clearly horrifying piece of infrastructure
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the casual professionalism — 'cadaver chute' sounds like official terminology delivered by someone who has completely normalized it. The reaction beat from April (implied) and the pure horror of the concept dressed in bureaucratic language is effective dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Jeremy, come on. Remember what we had? I miss you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: Tammy, we're done. It's over.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: I'll do anything. Anything you want. I'll quit my job, move to your apartment, cook every meal...

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: That doesn't sound better, that sounds worse.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Fine. I'll pay YOU. I'll give you money. Every week. How much do you want?

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: No, Tammy—

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: A car! I'll buy you a car! A nice one! A BMW!

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: I don't want your car.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Then I'll commit a crime. I'll rob a bank. We'll go to jail together. At least we'd be together.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: Please stop talking.

jokes.text: So this is where you wanna eat lunch? In a steakhouse? Don't you have irritable bowel syndrome? / God, I hate that I know that.
jokes.setup: Leslie has arranged to meet Jamm to work on breaking him from Tammy's influence
jokes.punchline: Leslie casually knows about Jamm's IBS, and her immediate disgust at possessing this information is the second layer
jokes.explanation: 'God, I hate that I know that' is a perfect self-aware closer — Leslie's encyclopedic knowledge of everyone in Pawnee includes medical details she wishes she didn't have. The IBS detail for a steakhouse meeting adds good cringe texture.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's the power of willpower. No device necessary.

jokes.text: Yeah, it's murder on the old plumbing. But Tammy only wants me to eat steak and whiskey. She has my stool analyzed just to keep me honest.
jokes.setup: Leslie has pointed out the obvious problem of IBS and steak
jokes.punchline: Jamm reveals Tammy has him on a steak-and-whiskey diet AND analyzes his stool to ensure compliance
jokes.explanation: Tammy Two's stool-analysis protocol is a genuinely inspired detail — it's obsessive, controlling, medical, and insane simultaneously. 'Just to keep me honest' as the deadpan framing suggests Tammy has presented this as a normal relationship expectation. Dark and specific.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Saturn's Return is a real astrological event that happens every 29.5 years. It affects your life in profound ways.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: When I went through mine, I made some decisions I'm not proud of. Let's just say there's a reason I can never go back to Estonia.

jokes.text: It seems like Tammy is trying to turn you into Ron. And you're Jeremy Jamm! I mean, come on. You love Porsches and spiked iced tea. And you have a Hooters platinum card.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to reconnect Jamm with his identity to break Tammy's hold
jokes.punchline: The specific details of Jamm's authentic self — Porsches, spiked iced tea, a Hooters platinum card — are presented as things worth fighting for
jokes.explanation: The comedy works on two levels: Leslie earnestly championing someone's right to be their shallow, pathetic self, and the specific details chosen (spiked iced tea, Hooters PLATINUM card) being simultaneously tacky and oddly specific. Leslie fighting for Jamm's right to be Jamm is a great inversion.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: April is my friend.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, I'm not.

jokes.text: I mean, sure, I'm depressed, and I'm constantly sick, and nothing really brings me joy. But it just feels right.
jokes.setup: Jamm is defending his relationship with Tammy despite Leslie's concerns
jokes.punchline: He lists clinical depression, constant illness, and total joylessness as relationship features, then concludes 'but it just feels right'
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent — a list of objectively terrible things followed by 'but it just feels right' parodies the way people justify clearly destructive relationships. The specificity of the symptoms (depressed, constantly sick, nothing brings joy) against the romantic conclusion is well-calibrated. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not your friend. I don't care about you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know you do.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, I don't. Stop saying that.

jokes.text: Help me, Knope. I used to be so great. Remember? Everybody thought so. / Well...
jokes.setup: Jamm, finally broken, pleads with Leslie to help him escape Tammy
jokes.punchline: He claims he 'used to be so great' and that 'everybody thought so'; Leslie's pause before 'Well...' suggests this is not quite accurate
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in Leslie's 'Well...' — a single word that diplomatically refuses to confirm Jamm's self-assessment. Her relationship with honesty (she's trying to help him) vs. her inability to lie about him being 'great' is a perfect character moment.

jokes.text: Hey, look at that. More hair came out.
jokes.setup: Jamm is having an emotional breakdown as Leslie tells him how broken he is
jokes.punchline: In the middle of the emotional scene, Jamm notices his hair falling out — presented as a casual curiosity rather than a crisis
jokes.explanation: The 'More' in 'more hair came out' is doing a lot of work — it implies this has been happening gradually and Jamm has normalized it. The casual, curious tone while experiencing stress alopecia is exactly the kind of oblivious character detail that makes Jamm fascinating.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Five-second rule! Five-second rule!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This is still good. This is still good!

jokes.text: And obviously, everyone's in a really great mood now because of the Cubs winning the series.
jokes.setup: Andy and Tom are eating with Lucy in Chicago; the conversation turns to how the city has been
jokes.punchline: Andy mentions the Cubs winning the World Series (set in 2017) as current context — the show is set slightly in the future from its airing date
jokes.explanation: The show is set in 2017 and this reference to the Cubs winning is a future-set gag (2016 Cubs curse-breaking) that was a real event by the time the show aired. It functions as a low-key meta-joke about the show's time-skip. The rewatch bonus comes from rewatching after the Cubs actually won.

jokes.text: Gryzzl came in, they gave everyone free tablets and Wi-Fi and phones. You can watch Hitch 2 anytime, anywhere! Finally! That's the dream.
jokes.setup: Andy is describing how Pawnee has changed with Gryzzl's arrival
jokes.punchline: The ultimate pinnacle of free technology access is watching 'Hitch 2' — a sequel that doesn't exist — anytime
jokes.explanation: The future-set joke about Hitch 2 existing is both a comment on Hollywood sequels and Andy's specific taste level. 'That's the dream' from Lucy (who seems more sophisticated) adds to the absurdity of agreeing. The specificity of Hitch rather than a generic sequel choice is the right call.

jokes.text: Dammit, Ron! Engage in the culture once in a while!
jokes.setup: Leslie has used Monsters, Inc. as an example to make a point about monsters having souls; Ron says he hasn't seen it
jokes.punchline: Leslie's exasperation explodes into 'Engage in the culture once in a while!' — treating watching a Pixar movie as a civic responsibility
jokes.explanation: The specific charge — 'engage in the culture' — framed as moral obligation is a perfect Leslie construction. She treats pop culture consumption as a shared social responsibility, which is both funny in itself and a rich character insight. The line has strong standalone quotability.

jokes.text: Jeremy. This is a gold bar. / You keep that in your desk?
jokes.setup: Ron produces a gold bar from his desk as an incentive for Jamm
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'You keep that in your desk?' — the gold bar's existence is the joke, as is Leslie's immediate practical confusion
jokes.explanation: Ron keeping gold bars in his desk is completely consistent with his anti-banking libertarian character and requires zero explanation for fans. The visual gag (a literal gold bar appearing in an office context) and Leslie's instinctive practical question are well-paired.

jokes.text: I will give you this gold bar if you say one unflattering thing about Tammy. / If I do, does Tammy get to keep the gold?
jokes.setup: Ron offers Jamm a gold bar as incentive to break from Tammy's hold
jokes.punchline: Jamm's first thought is whether Tammy gets to keep the gold if he takes it — his conditioning is so complete he can't conceptualize wealth outside her control
jokes.explanation: This is a precise, devastating joke about how thoroughly Tammy has broken Jamm. The question isn't 'can I keep it?' but 'does Tammy get to keep it?' — he's already pre-surrendering any asset. The cringe-comedy and character work here is excellent. Ron and Leslie's horrified silence following is implied.

jokes.text: When it comes to Tammy, the code is the same as that of the battlefield. First, you leave no man behind. Second, you must protect yourself against chemical warfare. Tammy does not abide by the Geneva Convention.
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining his approach to dealing with Tammy Two
jokes.punchline: He applies literal military doctrine to his ex-wife situation, culminating in 'Tammy does not abide by the Geneva Convention'
jokes.explanation: The Geneva Convention line is exceptional — it implies that Tammy's behavior in romantic conflict is so extreme it violates international laws of war. The escalation from 'leave no man behind' to 'chemical warfare' to 'Geneva Convention' is perfectly structured. This is the kind of Ron-specific absurdist deadpan that the show does at its very best. High quotability.

jokes.text: First, this is a chastity belt that I made by hand. It might be a couple sizes too big for you, but you can just pad it.
jokes.setup: Ron has produced his 'Tammy deprogramming kit' and is presenting its contents
jokes.punchline: The first item is a hand-crafted chastity belt — Ron made it himself, which is somehow the most Ron detail possible. The sizing note adds cringe.
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. Ron made a chastity belt BY HAND — the craftsmanship detail is perfect for his character (he can build anything). The practical sizing note ('it might be a couple sizes too big, but you can just pad it') treats this as completely normal problem-solving. The joke is character-specific to a degree that almost nothing in the episode matches. Reaches the 8+ threshold convincingly.

jokes.text: The first step is to cut out all sex. / That won't be necessary. We haven't done the deed yet. She lets me rub up against her leg sometimes.
jokes.setup: Ron outlines the first step of the deprogramming protocol: no sex
jokes.punchline: Jamm reveals they haven't had sex yet — and his description of 'rub up against her leg' as a consolation prize is both pathetic and specific
jokes.explanation: The revelation that Tammy hasn't slept with Jamm yet is darkly funny — she's been controlling him completely on the promise alone. 'She lets me rub up against her leg sometimes' is a beautifully sad and specific detail that captures their imbalanced dynamic perfectly.

jokes.text: She knows she has that card left to play, and you best believe she will.
jokes.setup: Jamm says the chastity belt is unnecessary because they haven't had sex
jokes.punchline: Ron's knowing, grim prediction about Tammy's tactical deployment of sex as a power move — delivered like a military briefing
jokes.explanation: Ron's PTSD-informed knowledge of Tammy's tactics — framed as strategic warfare analysis — is consistently the episode's funniest vein. His certainty here is darkly hilarious.

jokes.text: Ron is holding Tammy's perfume, Girth.
jokes.setup: Leslie is narrating the Pavlovian conditioning exercise
jokes.punchline: Tammy's perfume is named 'Girth' — the name itself is the joke
jokes.explanation: A single word doing maximum work. 'Girth' as a perfume name is perfectly disgusting — it implies exactly what Tammy's appeal is without spelling it out. The casual way Leslie mentions it (as if it's obvious) is the right delivery. One of the episode's sharpest single-word jokes.

jokes.text: Oh. It smells good. / Again. / Tammy. How many times are we gonna do this? / Until the bottle is empty. Again.
jokes.setup: The Pavlovian conditioning exercise involves exposing Jamm to Tammy's perfume and saying her name while Ron expresses disgust
jokes.punchline: Jamm keeps smelling it and saying it smells good; Ron must repeat the exercise until the bottle is empty
jokes.explanation: The running gag structure works — Jamm's inability to be conditioned (he keeps enjoying the smell) and Ron's resigned 'Until the bottle is empty' creates a good comedic loop. The futility is the joke.

jokes.text: Why is every job just paperwork? / Hey, it's a living.
jokes.setup: April learns that mortuary work also involves extensive paperwork and bureaucracy before any of the interesting parts
jokes.punchline: Dan responds to April's frustration about paperwork with 'Hey, it's a living' — a mortuary-specific pun delivered obliviously
jokes.explanation: Another Dan mortuary pun — 'it's a living' in a mortuary context. Like the 'dying to get in' joke, this is deliberately hacky punnery that works within the context of establishing Dan as a person who deploys terrible death puns. Slightly better landing than 'dying to get in' because of the irony context (April's frustration), but still low-craft.

jokes.text: I'm just gonna stay at my current job until I get old and die and then end up here, being embalmed by some weirdo who had to go to school for three years just to cut my guts open.
jokes.setup: April has concluded that mortuary work also isn't for her and is summing up her existential situation
jokes.punchline: Her bleak life-arc summary — 'stay at job until die, end up here' — delivered with April's flat certainty, with the specific 'weirdo' insult for the mortician who is standing right there
jokes.explanation: April's fatalistic life-summary delivered in front of the mortician she's just insulted is excellent character comedy. The logical completeness of her arc (job → death → embalmed by Dan) combined with her casual cruelty toward Dan creates a strong double-beat. Characteristically April in its dark specificity.

jokes.text: 'Hey there, horsey. Time to mount up and ride on into Bonertown. What do you say we get stanky in that pet store bathroom, Jamm?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is role-playing as Tammy for a training exercise to help Jamm resist her seduction
jokes.punchline: Leslie's approximation of Tammy's seduction — 'Bonertown,' 'get stanky in that pet store bathroom' — is a perfect parody of Tammy's specific brand of gross sexuality
jokes.explanation: 'Bonertown' and 'get stanky in that pet store bathroom' are the kind of specific, disgusting location comedy that elevates this beyond generic crude humor. Leslie Knope delivering Tammy Two's seduction script is the perfect character collision. The pet store bathroom as a chosen venue is inspired — it's exactly degrading enough for Tammy. Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'There will be no sex today, Tammy.' / Oh! / 'Instead, why don't you go into the pet store and feed yourself to the snakes. To hell with you woman, goodbye.'
jokes.setup: Ron is role-playing the ideal Jamm response to Tammy's seduction
jokes.punchline: Ron's scripted response escalates from refusal to suggesting she be fed to snakes, ending with his signature 'To hell with you woman, goodbye'
jokes.explanation: 'Feed yourself to the snakes' (continuing the pet store bathroom geography) and 'To hell with you woman, goodbye' as Ron's standardized Tammy rejection script is excellent. 'To hell with you woman, goodbye' has the quality of a practiced speech he has actually delivered. Strong quotability.

jokes.text: "There will be no sex today, Tammy." / "Instead, why don't you go into the pet store and feed yourself to the snakes?" / "To hell with you, woman, goodbye."
jokes.setup: Ron is performing the model Jamm response to Tammy's advances
jokes.punchline: Ron's scripted Jamm response escalates from refusal to suggesting she feed herself to snakes — a Ron Swanson-flavored insult that only emerges when he's playing another character
jokes.explanation: 'Go feed yourself to the snakes' and 'To hell with you, woman, goodbye' are pure Ron Swanson — the formal, declarative dismissal and the specificity of snake-feeding as a suggested course of action. The fact that Ron is theoretically playing Jamm but keeps injecting his own register is the meta-joke. 'To hell with you, woman, goodbye' is extremely quotable.

jokes.text: 'Hey ya big hunk of wiener meat. I've got forty hand towels, some energy bars, and a Chinese finger trap. Let's get gross.'
jokes.setup: Second round of Tammy seduction role-play with escalated props
jokes.punchline: 'Forty hand towels, some energy bars, and a Chinese finger trap' as Tammy's seduction kit — the specificity of 40 towels and the Chinese finger trap as a 'gross' device
jokes.explanation: The forty hand towels (implying industrial-scale clean-up) and the Chinese finger trap (its purpose left to the imagination) make this a masterwork of comedic implication. 'Let's get gross' as the sign-off is perfectly Tammy. The number forty specifically, not 'a bunch,' is exactly the right comedic choice. One of the episode's top jokes.

jokes.text: What are you wearing? / It's a crotch blinder of my own design. In this scenario, she will be coming at you pants-less.
jokes.setup: Ron has produced something to help Jamm resist Tammy's visual appeal
jokes.punchline: 'Crotch blinder of my own design' — Ron has invented and hand-crafted a specialized piece of equipment for this exact scenario, which he has clearly thought through extensively
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'crotch blinder of my own design' is one of the episode's best lines. It combines: Ron's craftsman identity (he made it himself), his tactical seriousness (it exists to solve a specific defensive problem), and the absurdity of needing such a device. 'Of my own design' implies he researched whether such a product existed commercially and found nothing adequate. This is premium character-specific comedy. Near-top mark for the episode.

jokes.text: Okay, the doors are locked, windows secured, there is no way Tammy's getting in here. / 'Jamm! Strip down, you sex maggot!'
jokes.setup: Leslie declares the room secured against Tammy
jokes.punchline: Tammy immediately appears, having entered via the armoire — called a 'sex maggot' as her opener
jokes.explanation: 'Strip down, you sex maggot' is an exceptional insult — 'sex maggot' implies someone who squirms and feeds in sexual situations, which is both gross and oddly precise. The subversion of Leslie's confident 'no way she's getting in' landing immediately with Tammy's entrance is perfect structure.

jokes.text: And hold! What was your mistake? / You didn't check the armoire. / Tammy once camped out in my attic for six days awaiting my arrival. She survived on rats and rainwater.
jokes.setup: Tammy has breached the room through the armoire; Leslie calls a training halt
jokes.punchline: Ron's explanation — she survived in his attic for six days on rats and rainwater — presents Tammy as a feral, almost supernatural predator
jokes.explanation: The six-day attic ambush sustained on rats and rainwater is a genuinely inspired piece of backstory. It escalates Tammy's mythology from 'manipulative ex' to 'survivor-level predator.' The specificity of 'rats and rainwater' (implying she hunted the rats) is the kind of specific absurd detail that defines great character comedy.

jokes.text: One XXL, one kid's XL. / Hey! You remembered my size!
jokes.setup: Lucy brings merchandise for Tom and Andy
jokes.punchline: Andy wears a kid's XL — and his delighted recognition that she remembered implies this is a normal, established fact about him
jokes.explanation: Andy's genuine pride that Lucy remembered his kid's XL size is the kind of small character-consistent detail that makes Parks great. His complete lack of embarrassment about wearing children's clothing is perfectly Andy.

jokes.text: I was wondering would you wanna maybe... Come work for me in Pawnee?
jokes.setup: Tom has been building up courage to ask Lucy something — Andy has been coaching him to 'make his move' and 'ask her out'
jokes.punchline: The camera (and audience and Andy) expect a romantic ask; Tom chickens out and offers her a job
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is well-executed — the long pause before 'Come work for me in Pawnee?' perfectly captures Tom chickening out and pivoting to professional safety. It's a character-true moment (Tom's fear of rejection) that uses structure to maximize the comedy.

jokes.text: I mean, I'd have to talk to my boyfriend about it first... / Yeah, of course! This is all perfect, and everything's worked out just as I'd hoped.
jokes.setup: Tom has just learned Lucy has a boyfriend
jokes.punchline: Tom's immediate, enthusiastic 'This is all perfect, and everything's worked out just as I'd hoped' is delivered with clear insincerity as his face falls
jokes.explanation: The over-commitment to false enthusiasm ('just as I'd hoped') while clearly devastated is a well-timed ironic beat. The formal completeness of the sentence ('this is all perfect') when things are clearly not perfect is the comedy engine here.

jokes.text: I'd have to talk to my boyfriend about it first. / Yeah, of course! This is all perfect, and everything's worked out just as I'd hoped.
jokes.setup: Tom's romantic gambit has become a job offer; Lucy reveals she has a boyfriend
jokes.punchline: Tom's immediate 'Yeah, of course! This is all perfect, and everything's worked out just as I'd hoped' — delivered through what must be visible devastation
jokes.explanation: Tom's overcorrection into positivity after learning about the boyfriend is good character comedy — he's maintaining face while clearly imploding. 'Everything's worked out just as I'd hoped' while it very clearly hasn't is perfect ironic understatement.

jokes.text: Hey, this is why they call it Beantown, huh?
jokes.setup: Tom has just received devastating news about Lucy's boyfriend
jokes.punchline: Andy's contribution to the emotionally charged moment is pointing out that they're in Chicago, which is nicknamed Beantown (except it's not — that's Boston)
jokes.explanation: A callback to Andy's earlier geography confusion — he called Chicago 'the big apple' before, and now calls it 'Beantown' (Boston's nickname). The emotional disconnect (Tom is devastated, Andy is thinking about beans) and the continued wrong-city-nickname running gag combine perfectly.

jokes.text: That's 'cause you're my widdle baby! / We drilled you on this, Jamm! Baby talk, what do you do? / I'm not a baby! I'm a big boy!
jokes.setup: Tammy responds to Jamm's breakup attempt with infantilizing baby talk; Leslie calls back their training
jokes.punchline: Jamm's trained response to baby talk is 'I'm not a baby! I'm a big boy!' — which sounds exactly like something a baby would say
jokes.explanation: The training callback pays off brilliantly — Jamm's scripted response sounds almost identical to what a baby would say. The irony of the anti-baby-talk script being toddler language is perfect. Leslie's 'Yeah, okay. Well, that wasn't terrible' as coaching feedback is also a nice beat.

jokes.text: Tammy, I've given this a lot of thought. We should break up. / What's the matter, little boy? Did the bad people get to you?
jokes.setup: Jamm attempts to break up with Tammy after his deprogramming
jokes.punchline: Tammy's baby-talk response — 'little boy,' 'bad people' — immediately infantilizes him, attacking exactly the power dynamic Leslie tried to fix
jokes.explanation: Tammy's tactical deployment of baby talk is excellent character work — she identifies the correct counter-move instantly. 'Did the bad people get to you?' as her framing of Leslie and Ron's deprogramming is darkly funny.

jokes.text: We drilled you on this, Jamm! Baby talk, what do you do? / I'm not a baby! I'm a big boy!
jokes.setup: Jamm is failing against Tammy's baby talk despite deprogramming training
jokes.punchline: Jamm's 'resistance' to baby talk is to declare 'I'm not a baby! I'm a big boy!' — which is itself baby talk, and exactly what a baby would say
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke. Jamm's counter to baby talk is to respond in baby talk — 'I'm a big boy' is exactly what a toddler says. The irony is total: in trying not to be treated as a baby, he has confirmed his baby status. Leslie's exasperated 'Yeah, okay. Well, that wasn't terrible' adds a perfect understatement layer. High structure, character integration, and economy.

jokes.text: How's this, Leslie? You leave us alone, and we swing the vote to you. Help you get your park. / No. Nice try. Stay strong, Jeremy.
jokes.setup: Tammy tries to bribe Leslie with the very thing she came for — the vote
jokes.punchline: Leslie refuses, turning down the bribe that would achieve her stated goal — a genuine character moment played for comedic nobility
jokes.explanation: The joke is Leslie's incorruptibility — she could get what she wants but refuses to get it through Tammy. The comedy is character-based: we expected Leslie to waver, and she doesn't. 'Nice try' has perfect dismissive economy.

jokes.text: It's been long enough. What do you say we consummate our relationship tonight?
jokes.setup: Jamm has stood firm in ending the relationship; Tammy has run out of manipulation options
jokes.punchline: Tammy deploys the final card — sex — exactly as Ron predicted she would
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Ron's earlier prediction — the 'last card' moment — works because we've been waiting for it. The comedy is in the inevitability Ron forecast coming true precisely as described.

jokes.text: Ron. I need that crotch blinder! / No, you don't. Just end it.
jokes.setup: Tammy has deployed the sex offer and Jamm is struggling to resist
jokes.punchline: Jamm desperately calls for the crotch blinder; Ron refuses — treating it as a crutch rather than a solution
jokes.explanation: The callback works because Ron withholding the crotch blinder becomes an act of tough-love coaching. 'No, you don't. Just end it.' is Ron at his most stoic-mentor. The crotch blinder reappearing as an emotional crutch is both a callback payoff and a joke about dependency.

jokes.text: Look at my boobs. / No. / Look downstairs. / No. / There's a prize inside for you. / It's over, Tammy.
jokes.setup: Tammy is attempting to seduce Jamm with a rapid escalating series of offers
jokes.punchline: Each offer is refused with a flat 'No'; 'There's a prize inside for you' is Tammy's most deranged offer
jokes.explanation: 'There's a prize inside for you' is extraordinary — the gamification of sex as a Kinder Egg-style prize reveal is specific, surreal, and uniquely Tammy. The escalating 'No' responses build the rhythm perfectly. The deadpan refusals against increasingly bizarre offers is excellent structure.

jokes.text: Turns out the crotch blinder was inside you all along.
jokes.setup: Jamm has successfully ended things with Tammy without using the crotch blinder
jokes.punchline: Leslie's sincere inspirational-speech framing of 'the crotch blinder was inside you all along' — a parody of 'the courage was inside you all along' tropes
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke and one of Parks and Recreation's finest single-line payoffs. The formal structure — the sincere inspirational-speech form ('the X was inside you all along') applied to the crotch blinder — is perfect. It requires the full setup of Ron inventing the device, Jamm nearly needing it, and the moral arc of the scene to land. The comedy builds perfectly through the episode. Leslie delivering it as genuine wisdom is everything. This is the anchor joke of the episode — clearly exceptional, and in the company of the show's best moments. The 9.5 impact score reflects the room erupting.

jokes.text: Come on, everybody! Who wants to get it on? I'm naked.
jokes.setup: Jamm has rejected Tammy and she has lost; the group has won
jokes.punchline: Tammy immediately pivots to propositioning the entire group; she is already naked
jokes.explanation: Tammy's completely unashamed pivot — total defeat processed as 'open casting call' — is perfectly in character. 'I'm naked' as the capper (she's apparently already disrobed in preparation) is economical and funny. A good button for the Tammy scene.

jokes.text: Saturn's Return. / What? / Saturn's orbit around the sun takes roughly 29 years, and when it gets back to where it was when you were born, lots of turmoil, self-discovery. When I was your age, I got banned from every riverboat in Germany.
jokes.setup: April is having an existential crisis about her career direction
jokes.punchline: Donna's explanation of Saturn's Return is delivered as genuine wisdom, then immediately undermined by the revelation that her own Saturn's Return resulted in being banned from German riverboats
jokes.explanation: Donna's cosmic explanation is presented as sage wisdom, but 'I got banned from every riverboat in Germany' as the illustrative personal example is a perfect comedic collapse. The specificity of 'every riverboat' (plural, implying a campaign rather than an incident) and 'in Germany' (implying she went to Germany specifically for this) makes it exceptional. Donna's casual delivery seals it.

jokes.text: Oh, you know. Just regionally directing the Midwest whatever of who cares. / Isn't it great? Can you believe that they pay me for this? Because I would do this for free. / Jeez! / I do miss you, Terry.
jokes.setup: Terry runs into April and Donna, asks what April is up to
jokes.punchline: April gives a nihilistic non-title; Terry misinterprets her sarcasm as enthusiasm and doubles down with genuine positivity about doing it 'for free'; Donna's 'I do miss you, Terry' implies she hasn't seen him in a while despite apparently working together
jokes.explanation: Terry's eternal misreading of the room — taking April's deadpan nihilism as enthusiasm — is well-deployed. 'Midwest whatever of who cares' as a job title is a great April construction. Donna's casual 'I do miss you, Terry' (implying he's easy to forget even when present) is a nice button.

jokes.text: Okay, but you can't tell Leslie I might leave. She'll have a heart attack. Promise?
jokes.setup: April has asked Ben to keep her career uncertainty secret
jokes.punchline: The hyperbole of Leslie having a literal heart attack over job news — but delivered by April as a genuine concern, not melodrama
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Leslie genuinely WOULD have a disproportionate reaction, making 'heart attack' feel not entirely like hyperbole. Functional character comedy but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: No, I'm not. I've never cared for you.
jokes.setup: Ben has said April is his friend and he wants her to be happy 'because you're my friend'
jokes.punchline: April's immediate denial that they are friends — 'I've never cared for you' — delivered flatly as she absorbs his genuine kindness
jokes.explanation: This is a near-perfect April line. The emotional beat — Ben is being genuine and warm — is met with complete deadpan denial, which is the only way April can receive sincere affection. But the joke works precisely BECAUSE we know she's lying, which makes it both funny and touching. 'I've never cared for you' as a term of endearment is quintessentially April. Very high quotability.

jokes.text: Saturn's Return. [April repeats this to Ron Swanson as explanation for her strange behavior]
jokes.setup: Ron has observed April behaving strangely and asks for explanation
jokes.punchline: April repeats Donna's 'Saturn's Return' explanation as if it is fully sufficient — and given Ron's reaction, he apparently accepts it
jokes.explanation: A callback that works economically — two words, perfect delivery, treated as a complete explanation. Ron accepting it without question is a good non-verbal beat. The brevity elevates it.

jokes.text: Hey, Brokemons. I just wanted to let you know that I will be abstaining from the vote today. You are my two all-time best friends. And you brought me back from the brink.
jokes.setup: Jamm announces he won't vote either way
jokes.punchline: 'Brokemons' as his address for Leslie and Ron — a Pokémon portmanteau — and him calling them his 'two all-time best friends' when they have spent years as enemies
jokes.explanation: 'Brokemons' is an inventive portmanteau for Jamm and works as a character beat — he's the kind of person who'd use this. The irony of calling Leslie and Ron his best friends is good. 'Back from the brink' overstating a minor interpersonal intervention is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Hey, Brokemons. I just wanted to let you know that I will be abstaining from the vote today. You are my two all-time best friends. And you brought me back from the brink. So, I can't choose sides. Although, if I had to pick one side, it would be Lucy Liu's backside.
jokes.setup: Jamm delivers a heartfelt speech about friendship and abstaining from the vote
jokes.punchline: The sincere moment ends with 'it would be Lucy Liu's backside' — Jamm's version of a compliment is a butt reference
jokes.explanation: The emotional pivot — Jamm attempting to be moving, then revealing his emotional ceiling by ending on a celebrity butt reference — is perfect character comedy. 'Brokemons' as his affectionate term for Leslie and Ron is also a good detail. The joke shows Jamm has grown slightly while remaining fundamentally Jamm.

jokes.text: So, I can't choose sides. Although, if I had to pick one side, it would be Lucy Liu's backside.
jokes.setup: Jamm explains he can't vote because both Leslie and Ron are his best friends
jokes.punchline: The 'sides' wordplay pivots to a crass non-sequitur about Lucy Liu's backside — Jamm being Jamm
jokes.explanation: The wordplay is functional but cheap — pivoting from 'sides' to 'backside' with a celebrity name drop. Character-appropriate for Jamm but not impressive writing. The joke earns its score for character integration only.

jokes.text: I thought it was very big of you to not bend when Tammy promised you the vote. / Well, I thought it was very big of you to help him at all. You didn't have to do that.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron have a rare moment of mutual respect after the Jamm situation
jokes.punchline: Both acknowledge each other's decency before immediately snapping back to adversarial mode
jokes.explanation: The warmth of the mutual acknowledgment is the setup for the snap-back joke. The emotional beat plays primarily as character rather than comedy, but the subversion is present.

jokes.text: I still don't know what 'claiming allowances' means. I always just put six. / So far, so good. / Dude, you are totally going to jail.
jokes.setup: Tom is starting his new life; the conversation turns to practical adulting matters
jokes.punchline: Tom has been randomly putting '6' on tax forms he doesn't understand; Andy is supportive; Lucy's 'you're totally going to jail' deflates both
jokes.explanation: The three-beat rhythm is efficient: Tom's confession, Andy's oblivious support, Lucy's clear-eyed verdict. 'I always just put six' as a tax strategy is relatable stupidity elevated by the specificity of the number.

jokes.text: This couldn't have worked out any better. There was a guy eating lunch in here who didn't finish his spaghetti.
jokes.setup: Andy is summing up how well things have worked out for Tom
jokes.punchline: His measure of 'couldn't have worked out any better' includes finding abandoned spaghetti — on equal footing with Tom's personal and professional developments
jokes.explanation: Andy's value system — in which leftover spaghetti is a genuine boon equal to or greater than human connection — is a perfect character encapsulation. The deadpan placement alongside the emotional resolution of the episode is the ideal button. 'There was a guy eating lunch in here who didn't finish his spaghetti' as a closing life-assessment is quintessentially Andy Dwyer.

jokes.text: Five-second rule! [Andy presumably diving for/eating the abandoned spaghetti]
jokes.setup: Andy has mentioned the unfinished spaghetti
jokes.punchline: The episode ends on Andy invoking the five-second rule for floor spaghetti in a restaurant
jokes.explanation: A solid tag — the button on the button. Andy eating restaurant floor spaghetti is the logical, entirely believable extension of his character. The five-second rule in a restaurant context is the right level of gross. Not exceptional writing but a fitting final image.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ron briefly put aside their feud to help old foe Jeremy Jamm escape the clutches of the diabolical Tammy 2. Ben vows to help April discover her true passion in life, while Andy and Tom travel to Chicago.
insight: Ron's absurd woodworking obsession drives 54 jokes at pedestrian density, coasting on character comfort rather than craft.
